subChunks.title: try/catch/finally & Exception Hierarchy
subChunks.hookHtml: A spell can misfire. A file can be missing. A user can type letters when you expect numbers. In Java, exceptions are the formal mechanism for signalling and handling these errors gracefully.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
try / catch / finally

try {
    // code that might throw
    int result = 10 / 0;
} catch (ArithmeticException e) {
    System.out.println("Cannot divide by zero: " + e.getMessage());
} finally {
    System.out.println("This always runs — cleanup here.");
}

finally runs whether or not an exception was thrown — ideal for closing resources.

Multiple catch blocks

try {
    String s = null;
    System.out.println(s.length()); // NullPointerException
    int[] arr = new int[5];
    arr[10] = 1;                    // ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
} catch (NullPointerException e) {
    System.out.println("Null reference: " + e.getMessage());
} catch (ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException e) {
    System.out.println("Array index error: " + e.getMessage());
} catch (Exception e) { // catches anything else
    System.out.println("Unknown error: " + e.getMessage());
}

The Exception hierarchy

Throwable
├── Error          (JVM errors — do not catch: OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError)
└── Exception
    ├── RuntimeException  (unchecked — compiler doesn't force handling)
    │   ├── NullPointerException
    │   ├── ArithmeticException
    │   ├── ClassCastException
    │   └── ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException
    └── IOException        (checked — compiler forces try/catch or throws declaration)
        ├── FileNotFoundException
        └── ...

Checked vs Unchecked

  • Checked exceptions (subclasses of Exception but not RuntimeException) — the compiler forces you to handle them with try/catch or declare throws in the method signature.
  • Unchecked exceptions (subclasses of RuntimeException) — compiler does not require handling; they represent programming errors.

storyBeats.text: During a practice duel, a student's spell misfires and shatters a training dummy. Eldrin calmly notes the failure in his ledger.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: In Java, when something goes wrong — dividing by zero, accessing a null reference, reading a file that doesn't exist — the JVM throws an exception. Without handling, your program crashes. With try and catch, you respond gracefully.

storyBeats.speaker: Basic try/catch
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Java's exceptions form a hierarchy rooted at Throwable. Error represents JVM catastrophes — never catch them. RuntimeException subclasses are your programming mistakes: NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. Checked exceptions like IOException represent external conditions the compiler forces you to acknowledge.

storyBeats.speaker: The hierarchy in practice
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Order your catch blocks from most specific to most general. Catching Exception before NullPointerException means the specific block is unreachable — the compiler will warn you.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Write a safe integer-division method:

  1. Create a method safeDivide(int a, int b) that returns the result of a / b.
  2. Wrap the division in a try/catch for ArithmeticException. If caught, print "Cannot divide by zero" and return -1.
  3. Add a finally block that prints "Division attempted".
  4. In main, call safeDivide(10, 2) and safeDivide(10, 0) and print both results.

options: Only when an exception is thrown
Only when no exception is thrown
Always, whether or not an exception occurs
Only when the catch block runs
questions.correctAnswer: Always, whether or not an exception occurs
questions.explanationHtml: finally always executes — it is the guaranteed cleanup section. The only exceptions are JVM crashes or System.exit() being called.

questions.questionHtml: A NullPointerException is a checked exception that the compiler requires you to handle.
questions.explanationHtml: NullPointerException is a subclass of RuntimeException, making it an unchecked exception. The compiler does not require a try/catch for it — you are expected to prevent it through proper null-checking.

questions.questionHtml: In which order should catch blocks be arranged?
questions.explanationHtml: Catch blocks are evaluated top-to-bottom. If Exception is listed first, it catches everything — the specific blocks below it are unreachable. Arrange from most specific (e.g., FileNotFoundException) to most general (Exception).

questions.questionHtml: A method reads from a file. Should it handle IOException internally or declare it with throws? When does each choice make sense?
questions.correctAnswer: Handle it internally if the method can recover (e.g., return a default value). Declare throws if the caller is better placed to decide how to handle the error. Declaring throws is often preferred in library code.
questions.explanationHtml: Neither is always correct. Use throws when the method cannot meaningfully recover and the caller has context to decide the right response. Handle internally when recovery is straightforward (log and return a default). Declaring throws in library APIs is often preferred because it does not impose one error-handling strategy on all callers.

subChunks.title: Custom Exceptions & try-with-resources
subChunks.hookHtml: Java's built-in exceptions cover common errors. But what about domain-specific failures — an invalid spell name, a player attempting to go below zero health? Custom exceptions make your error handling precise and self-documenting.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Creating custom exceptions

// Unchecked custom exception (extends RuntimeException)
public class InsufficientManaException extends RuntimeException {
    private final int required;
    private final int available;

    public InsufficientManaException(int required, int available) {
        super("Need " + required + " mana but only " + available + " available");
        this.required  = required;
        this.available = available;
    }

    public int getRequired()  { return required; }
    public int getAvailable() { return available; }
}

// Checked custom exception (extends Exception)
public class SpellNotFoundException extends Exception {
    public SpellNotFoundException(String spellName) {
        super("Spell not found: " + spellName);
    }
}

Throwing custom exceptions

public void castSpell(String spellName, int mana) throws SpellNotFoundException {
    if (!spellbook.contains(spellName)) {
        throw new SpellNotFoundException(spellName); // checked — caller must handle
    }
    if (mana < 20) {
        throw new InsufficientManaException(20, mana); // unchecked
    }
    System.out.println("Casting " + spellName);
}

try-with-resources (AutoCloseable)

Any class implementing AutoCloseable can be used in a try-with-resources block. Java automatically calls close() when the block exits:

// Without try-with-resources (error-prone):
BufferedReader br = null;
try {
    br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("file.txt"));
    String line = br.readLine();
} finally {
    if (br != null) br.close(); // easy to forget!
}

// With try-with-resources (modern, preferred):
try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader("file.txt"))) {
    String line = br.readLine();
    System.out.println(line);
} catch (IOException e) {
    System.out.println("Error: " + e.getMessage());
}
// br.close() is guaranteed — no finally needed

storyBeats.text: A student tries to cast a spell she hasn't learned yet. The magical registry throws a generic error — 'operation failed' — with no further detail. Eldrin sighs.

storyBeats.speaker: Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Generic exceptions are useless. SpellNotFoundException? Now that is informative. Create your own exception classes for your domain. A meaningful exception message means the next wizard to read the stack trace understands instantly what went wrong.

storyBeats.speaker: Custom exception
Archmage Eldrin
storyBeats.text: Now for one of Java's finest innovations: try-with-resources. Any object that holds an external resource — a file, a network connection, a database cursor — must be closed when done. Forgetting is a resource leak. The try (Resource r = ...) syntax closes it automatically, even if an exception is thrown.

storyBeats.speaker: try-with-resources

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
Create a custom unchecked exception InvalidSpellException that extends RuntimeException. Its constructor takes a String spellName and passes "Invalid spell: " + spellName to the super constructor.

Write a method cast(String spell) that throws InvalidSpellException if the spell is not in the set {"Fireball", "Heal", "Shield"}. Otherwise it prints "Casting: [spell]".

In main: try to cast "Heal" (valid) and "DarkRitual" (invalid). Wrap both calls in one try/catch for InvalidSpellException that prints the exception message.

questions.questionHtml: To create a checked custom exception, your class should extend:
questions.explanationHtml: Extending Exception (but not RuntimeException) creates a checked exception — the compiler requires callers to handle it. Extending RuntimeException creates an unchecked exception.

questions.questionHtml: In a try-with-resources block, close() is called only if no exception is thrown.
questions.explanationHtml: close() is called regardless of whether an exception was thrown — that is the whole point of try-with-resources. It replaces the error-prone try/finally pattern.

questions.codeSnippet:
if (value < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Negative: " + value);
System.out.println("OK");
questions.correctAnswer: Exception is thrown — 'OK' is never printed. IllegalArgumentException propagates to the caller.
questions.explanationHtml: throw immediately stops execution of the current method. Statements after throw are not reached. The exception propagates up the call stack until caught.

questions.questionHtml: When should you create a checked exception (extends Exception) rather than an unchecked one (extends RuntimeException)?
options: When the error is a programming mistake that should never happen in production
When the caller can reasonably recover and should be forced to consider the failure
When you want to log the error silently
When the error comes from the JVM rather than application code
questions.correctAnswer: When the caller can reasonably recover and should be forced to consider the failure
questions.explanationHtml: Use checked exceptions for recoverable conditions where the caller has a meaningful choice (file not found — prompt user to choose a different file). Use unchecked for programming errors (null argument to a method that documents it doesn't accept null). Checking everything leads to cluttered code; checking nothing hides recoverable conditions.
